name: Femur vs tibia lengthening

lead: Cosmetic leg lengthening in the looksmaxxing community is usually discussed as a choice between lengthening the femur (thigh bone), the tibia (shin bone), or both in stages. Forum users commonly describe the femur as the segment that yields more length and is done first, with the tibia added later for extra height.

Published literature on limb lengthening comes mainly from treatment of leg-length differences, trauma and skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia. It describes complications in both segments, but studies specifically comparing femur and tibia for purely cosmetic height gain are scarce.

paras: Both procedures cut the bone and then separate the ends gradually so new bone forms in the gap (distraction osteogenesis), using either an external frame or a motorised nail placed inside the bone marrow canal. The femur is surrounded by large muscles, whereas the tibia sits just under the skin with nerves and vessels running close to the ankle and foot.

Reported complications in limb lengthening in general include nerve injury, joint stiffness or contracture, delayed or failed bone healing, infection, and hardware problems. Descriptions in the literature associate femoral lengthening with knee stiffness and quadriceps tightness, and tibial lengthening with ankle and nerve-related problems. The procedure is elective in the cosmetic context and is generally not covered by insurance.

lead: Femur vs tibia lengthening refers, in looksmaxxing and limb-lengthening communities, to the decision about which bone segment to lengthen surgically for height: the femur (thigh bone), the tibia (shin bone), or both, usually in stages. Both operations use distraction osteogenesis, in which a bone is cut and the pieces are slowly pulled apart so that new bone forms in the gap, at a rate commonly given as about 1 mm per day [1].

Forum participants often describe the femur as the first-choice segment because it is said to allow more length per surgery and to be better tolerated, with tibial lengthening added later for those who want more height. An AI-generated encyclopedia summary reports typical cosmetic targets of roughly 5 to 8 cm per segment and notes that surgeons are described as more conservative with the tibia [2]; these figures have not been independently verified here and vary between sources.

Published clinical research on lengthening comes largely from reconstructive orthopaedics and skeletal dysplasia, where femur and tibia are lengthened for medical reasons [3][4]. Studies that compare the two segments for purely cosmetic height gain are limited, so most statements about relative risk in the cosmetic setting rest on surgeon experience and case series.

paras: In distraction osteogenesis the surgeon cuts the bone (an osteotomy), waits a latency period of about a week, then separates the ends gradually, followed by a consolidation period while the new bone hardens. Reviews describe a distraction rate of around 1 mm per day; separating too quickly is associated with failure of the new bone to form, and too slowly with premature union [1]. The Russian surgeon Gavriil Ilizarov, working from the 1950s, is credited with establishing the modern external-fixator technique and its distraction rates [1].

Methods have diversified from frames worn on the outside of the leg to combined and fully internal approaches. A comparative study of femoral lengthening reported that lengthening over a nail had fewer complications than an earlier internal kinetic-distraction device [5]. Motorised internal nails, including magnetically controlled retrograde femoral nails, have also been described in the medical literature [6]. Clinical trial registrations show ongoing post-market studies of one such magnetic nail system in patients with limb length discrepancy [7][8].

Online summaries describe the femur as the segment that tolerates the most lengthening, with one reporting typical cosmetic targets of about 6 to 8 cm [2]. Orthopaedic papers on femoral lengthening describe knee stiffness and quadriceps tightness as recognised problems; one case series describes a limited quadricepsplasty procedure used to treat contracture that developed during femoral lengthening [9].

The same summary describes tibial targets as more modest, around 4 to 6 cm, and states that the tibia carries higher risk to the ankle and knee [2]. Staged plans are described in which the femurs are done first and the tibias at least a year later [2]. Animal research has shown that denervation impairs bone regeneration in rabbit tibial lengthening, an experiment that points to the importance of intact nerve supply to the healing segment [10].

Simultaneous lengthening of both femurs and tibias has been studied in people with achondroplasia, including a registered trial of 22 patients [11]. A review of limb lengthening in achondroplasia describes substantial complication rates and notes that guidelines on timing and extent are not uniform around the world [4]. These populations differ from cosmetic patients in age, indication and bone quality.

A Grokipedia summary reports, from one series of 814 procedures, nerve injury in about 9 percent of limbs, joint contracture in up to roughly 5 percent of segments, and delayed or failed healing in a minority of nail cases, with higher rates reported at one specialist centre for cosmetic patients [2]. Because that source is AI-generated and its figures are internally inconsistent in places, they are best read as indicative only.

More generally, the published literature on distraction osteogenesis lists infection, hardware failure, healing problems and nerve injury among recognised complications [1]. A case report describes a pseudoaneurysm after high tibial osteotomy and limb lengthening [12]. A 2006 report states that China's Ministry of Health banned cosmetic limb lengthening after operations with serious side effects [1].

No clinical studies were found that directly compare femur against tibia lengthening for cosmetic height gain in healthy adults. Related human research covers limb lengthening for leg length discrepancy, trauma and achondroplasia, including a comparison of lengthening techniques in the femur [5], a series on achondroplasia [4], and registered trials of simultaneous femoral and tibial lengthening [11] and of a magnetic intramedullary lengthening system [7][8].

lore.intro: On height-focused forums the femur-or-tibia question is treated as a core planning decision, often framed as a trade-off between amount of height gained and risk to nerves and the ankle.

claims.claim: The femur gives more height with fewer complications, so it should come first.
Tibial lengthening carries more risk to nerves and the ankle.
Both bones can be lengthened together for a larger total gain.

timeline.event: Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical limb-lengthening attempt, with high complication rates [1]
Gavriil Ilizarov develops external fixation and defines distraction rates [1]
Registered study begins of simultaneous femoral and tibial lengthening in achondroplasia [11]
Comparison of lengthening over a nail versus an internal kinetic device in the femur published [5]
